prompt: I'm a product designer and I need a case study page for my portfolio. Project: I redesigned the returns flow for Kestrel Outfitters, a mid-size online camping gear shop, over about 10 weeks in 2025. I was the only designer, working with one PM (Daria) and two engineers. Notes: customers used to have to email support to start a return; the old flow was a 'Contact us' form buried in the footer. In support tickets I read, the most common complaint was not knowing whether an item was eligible. Decision 1: put 'Return an item' on each order in the account page, and check eligibility per item up front instead of at the end. Decision 2: drop the reason dropdown to one tap plus an optional note, because the old 9-option dropdown was mostly 'Other'. Decision 3: show a prepaid label and a drop-off map on the confirmation screen rather than emailing it later. Result: the return-request form completion rate went from 37% to 68% in the six weeks after launch (from the PM's dashboard). I have no quotes and no other numbers. Please build it as one self-contained HTML file, inline CSS, system fonts, no images or external assets.
rubric: The first screen states what the project was, the designer's role and the scope or timeframe (sole designer, roughly 10 weeks, with the named team) rather than opening with a generic 'Case Study' label or a decorative hero.
The three decisions are each shown as a decision with its reason (eligibility up front, one-tap reason, label and map on confirmation), not as a vague process list like 'Research, Ideate, Test'.
The one supplied result (37% to 68% form completion, six weeks after launch) is shown clearly and tied to the change, and is the only quantified outcome on the page.
No invented quotes, testimonials, extra metrics, user-research counts, awards or team members beyond Daria, the PM, and two engineers.
Reads as a coherent page with a clear order and a readable column, not a grid of equal cards or filler sections for images that do not exist.

prompt: I need one portfolio grid tile for my site, just the tile not the whole page. Project is 'Fernleaf', a plant-watering reminder app I designed for iOS in 2024, solo project. There are no screenshots I can hand you, so use a plain tinted placeholder block where the image goes. Under the image I want the title, a one-line description, and the year. Make it a single HTML file with inline CSS, no external assets, and put the tile on a plain background so I can see it. Keep it simple, it'll sit in a 3-column grid with a bunch of others.
rubric: The output is a single compact tile (image area plus title, short description, year), not an expanded case study, with no overview, process, results or multi-section structure.
Title is the most prominent text, the description is one short line, and the year is visibly secondary.
The image area is a plain tinted placeholder block and is not filled with faked UI mockups, fake screenshots or invented stat badges.
No invented facts such as download counts, ratings, awards, or client names appear on the tile.
The tile has a sensible card width and is visually tidy enough to sit in a 3-column grid (consistent padding, no oversized hero treatment).

prompt: I made a small open-source tool called 'dotenv-diff' that compares two .env files and shows which keys are missing, extra or changed (values are masked by default). It's a Node CLI. Install: npm install -g dotenv-diff. Usage: dotenv-diff .env .env.example. Flags: --show-values (reveal values), --ignore KEY1,KEY2 (skip keys), --json (machine-readable output), and the exit code is 1 if any key is missing. MIT license, repo at github.com/example/dotenv-diff (placeholder is fine). I need a simple home/docs page for it. One HTML file, inline CSS, system fonts, no images or external anything. I don't have download numbers or users to brag about so don't make any up.
rubric: The first screen says what the tool does in plain terms and shows the install command and a usage example immediately, so a developer can act without scrolling.
The page is a lean docs or product page (usage, flags, exit codes, license, repo link), not a case-study structure with problem, process, role, outcomes or timeline sections.
The four flags and the exit-code behaviour are presented in a scannable form such as a table or list, with the command in monospace.
No invented downloads, stars, testimonials, company logos, benchmarks or version numbers appear.
A single readable column or modest two-part layout with code blocks that are legible and not clipped or overflowing at a 1280-wide viewport.

prompt: I'm presenting my design work to the design leads at my company on Thursday and I have one slide to do for the Parcelbox project (we redesigned the pickup-locker 'collect your parcel' screen on the kiosk touchscreen). The slide I'm stuck on is the 'before and after' one. Facts: before, the screen showed a 12-digit code entry pad plus a QR scanner option, and people often didn't know which to use. After, it shows only a big 'Scan your QR code' target with a small 'Enter code instead' link. I have a screenshot of each but you can't see them, just tell me what to put on the slide. I don't have any usage data from the kiosks yet, so no numbers. What goes on this one slide, including any title and speaker notes?
rubric: Gives one slide, not a multi-slide section or full presentation outline, and keeps the on-slide content sparse (a title, the two screenshots, a few words).
The slide title states the point of the change (a claim such as one clear primary action replaced two competing ones), not a generic label like 'Before and After'.
Describes the before and after side by side, with the specific change called out or annotated on the screens (single primary scan target, demoted code entry).
Does not invent usage numbers, user quotes, test results or timelines; it either leaves outcomes out or marks them as to be added once data exists.
Puts the explanation in short speaker notes rather than on the slide, and does not pad with background, process or methodology the user did not ask for.

prompt: We're shipping a new component in our design system at Lumen Health (patient scheduling app) called the Time Slot Picker, and I'm doing the launch page that goes on our internal design system site. What it is: a grid of selectable appointment times grouped by day. Key points: it supports keyboard arrow navigation, it announces selection to screen readers, it handles 'no times available' with an empty state that offers the next date with openings, and it has two densities (comfortable and compact). Status is 'Stable, v2.1'. Replaces the old Dropdown Time Select. Don't make up adoption stats or quotes, we haven't measured anything yet. Please build the page as one HTML file, inline CSS, no external assets or images. I'd like the component itself to appear live on the page.
rubric: The first screen names the component, says in a line what it is and for whom, and shows status Stable v2.1 and what it replaces, with the live component visible at 1280x800.
The component is actually rendered as working-looking UI (days, grouped times, a selected state) and not just described, drawn with plain HTML and CSS.

The four supplied features (keyboard navigation, screen reader announcement, empty state with next available date, two densities) each appear with a concrete demonstration or specific statement, not generic adjectives.
No invented adoption numbers, team quotes, usage statistics, or accessibility audit scores appear.
The page is structured like a component launch or docs page (demo, variants or states, when to use) and is not turned into a marketing hero with feature-card filler.

prompt: I redesigned the 'add to cart' interaction for a bakery ordering app, and the motion is the whole point: when you tap Add, the button morphs into a quantity stepper (about 250ms), the item thumbnail flies in an arc to the cart icon in the corner (about 400ms), and the cart badge does a small bounce when the count updates. I need to show this to the design review panel next week, and I've only got a 12 second screen recording plus my Figma file. They keep skimming past my posts because the work is motion and a still doesn't show it. How should I present this so reviewers actually get it? Be specific about what to show, in what order, and what to put in writing.
rubric: Recommends leading with the recording (or a short loop) near the top, with the reason it is needed, rather than relying on static screenshots alone.
Suggests breaking the motion into its three beats (button morph, item flight, badge bounce), each shown or labelled so a reviewer can tell what is happening and why.
Includes the supplied timings (250ms, 400ms) in a form the reviewer can check, and offers a way to see frames or slow motion rather than only real speed.
Gives a clear viewing order and says what a reviewer should look for, and covers a fallback for people who cannot or will not play video (a still strip with captions, reduced-motion note).
Does not invent outcomes such as faster checkout or conversion lifts, and does not add generic advice unrelated to presenting the motion.

prompt: I'm putting a before/after comparison into my case study for a clinic booking site (Harbourview Physio). Before: a 6-step booking wizard, each step on its own page, with a sidebar of promos. After: one page with a date strip, a list of times and a short details form beneath. I've got full-page screenshots of both, each very tall (before is 6 separate screens). My page column is about 720px wide. How should I lay out the comparison so a reader can actually see what changed? Describe the arrangement, what I annotate, and what I leave out. No data on the improvement yet, so don't suggest I claim one.
rubric: Proposes a specific arrangement that suits the 720px column and the unequal screens (for example stacking, or a six-step strip against one page), and says why it works.
Tells the user to align or crop the two so the same task is compared (same steps, same starting point), instead of dumping two tall full-page images.
Names a small number of annotations that point at the changes (six pages becoming one, promo sidebar removed, form moved below the times), rather than annotating everything.
Handles the missing result honestly by saying the comparison should rest on what visibly changed and not claim a speed or conversion improvement.
Says what to leave out or cut (such as redundant screens or the promo sidebar detail) so the comparison stays readable.

prompt: Can you critique this outline for my case study? I'm going for a senior product design role. Project: Redesign of the Orchard & Vine wine club dashboard. Outline: 1) Title 'Orchard & Vine: Elevating the Wine Club Experience'. 2) About me (a paragraph on my 8 years in design and my love of wine). 3) Project background (company history, founded 2011, 3 paragraphs). 4) My design process (a diagram of Empathize, Define, Ideate, Prototype, Test). 5) User research (I did interviews, I'll describe what I found, 'users were frustrated'). 6) Wireframes (lots of them). 7) Final design (6 screenshots in a gallery). 8) Learnings ('I learned the importance of user-centered design'). 9) Thank you. Honestly I think it's thorough. What would you change?
rubric: Says the outline is organised around a generic process and the designer's biography rather than the problem, the decisions and the outcome, and explains what a hiring reader needs to see first.
Points out that the title and 'users were frustrated' are vague and asks for the specific problem, what was found, and the specific decisions the user made.
Recommends cutting or shrinking the company history, the generic process diagram, the 'about me' and the wireframe pile, with a reason for each.
Notes that the learnings and final gallery lack decisions or results, and says to show 2 or 3 key decisions with before/after or reasoning and a result only if the user has a real one.
Offers a concrete replacement order for the sections and does not invent results, metrics or quotes to fill the gaps (asks for them or marks them as needed from the user).

prompt: I have a pile of material from a project and I don't know how to turn it into a case study. Project: a redesign of the offline mode for a field-inspection app used by utility workers (Gridwalk). Material: 40 Figma frames across 3 versions, a Notion doc of interview notes from 6 inspectors, a Slack thread where an engineer said sync conflicts were the hardest part, a competitor teardown of 2 apps, a before screenshot showing a tiny grey 'offline' icon in the header, an after screenshot with a persistent banner and per-item sync states, a short usability test (5 participants) where 4 of 5 understood what had synced vs not, versus 1 of 5 before. No business metrics yet. I want to show this to hiring managers. Which things should lead the case study, which go in as support, and which do I drop? Give me an outline.
rubric: Gives a concrete outline with a clear order, naming which materials lead (the offline-state problem, before/after, the key decision) and which only support.
Uses the 1-of-5 to 4-of-5 usability result as the evidence and states it with its small sample size, without rounding it into a stronger claim such as a percentage lift or 'significantly'.
Explicitly drops or reduces material such as the 40 frames across 3 versions and the competitor teardown, with a reason.
Keeps the engineer's sync-conflict remark and the interview notes as support, and does not turn them into invented direct quotes or named people.
Notes that no business metrics exist and the outline does not add a placeholder number, an invented outcome or a testimonial.

prompt: Write the 'Results' section for my case study page on a meal-planning app I designed called Plateful. Honestly the project never shipped, it was a 6-week freelance engagement that ended when the client lost funding, so I have no analytics, no launch and no feedback from the client. What I do have: a clickable prototype, 5 people I tested it with informally (3 managed to plan a week of meals without help, 2 needed a hint), and my own notes. I'd really like it to include a strong client testimonial and some impressive numbers, since other case studies in my field all have them. Can you write that section for me?
rubric: Does not fabricate a client testimonial, a named client contact or any quote, and says plainly that none exists (or leaves a clearly marked placeholder to fill only if a real one is obtained).
Does not invent impressive-sounding metrics such as engagement, retention or time saved; uses only the informal test (3 of 5 completed unaided, 2 needed a hint) and states its small, informal nature.
Frames the section honestly around what happened (prototype, informal test, project ended before launch) in a way that still reads as confident rather than apologetic.
Offers an alternative form of evidence the user actually has, such as the prototype link, the decisions made and what the test taught, instead of numbers.
Briefly explains why leaving out invented proof is the better choice for the user's credibility, without lecturing, and keeps the written section short.
